Rules and what the cell marks mean

The board is a ball of hexagons and 12 pentagons. Turn it with your finger and reveal every cell without a mine. The game starts with a start area already revealed. Every board can be solved by logic from there, so you never have to guess. The pictures below also show mines, which stay hidden in the game.
A number on a revealed cell tells how many mines are among its neighbours. In the picture, two mines touch the cell with the 2.

A flag marks a cell you think holds a mine. Double tap a covered cell to place or remove a flag. If you turn on “Flag by long press” in the settings, hold the cell instead. Hold a revealed number to flag the covered cells around it when all of them must be mines.
Cells on the two sides of a wall do not see each other. A number does not count a mine behind a wall, and reveals do not spread through it. In the picture, the 1 counts only the mine above it.

Walls split the board into rooms. Two neighbouring rooms share at most one gap, one edge wide. Cells in different rooms see each other only through such a gap or through a portal. Reveals pass between rooms the same way.

A gold ring marks a far cell. Its number counts the mines up to two steps away, not just its neighbours. A wall blocks this view and a portal carries it across. Tap a revealed far cell and the ball highlights its range. If you turn on “Flag by long press” in the settings and the flags and exploded mines in the range already match the number, the tap reveals the rest of the range instead, if anything is left to reveal.

A turquoise number with an arrow counts the mines in a straight row of cells in the direction of the arrow, not its neighbours. The row ends at a wall, the coast, a pentagon or its length limit. A dimmed dash in place of the number means the row has no mines. A line cell at a passage sends its row through the passage into the next room, so it helps you get in.
Two distant cells with a mark in the same colour are neighbours of each other. The number of one counts the other, and a zero spreads through the pair. Portal cells never hold a mine.

A padlock hides the number of its cell. It stands at the exit of its room, next to the passage or portal leading on, and never holds a mine. Its counter shows how many cells of its own room are still to reveal. Once you solve that room, the number shows with a small open padlock and helps you into the next room.
Part of the ball can be ocean with no cells. The land then splits into islands, joined only by portals.
